clinicalPearls: Autosomal recessive; two genetic forms — kEDS-PLOD1 (deficiency of lysyl hydroxylase 1) and kEDS-FKBP14 (deficiency of the collagen chaperone FKBP22).
Core triad: congenital muscle hypotonia, congenital or early-onset progressive kyphoscoliosis, and generalised joint hypermobility with recurrent dislocations.
The PLOD1 form features scleral and ocular globe fragility with risk of rupture from minor trauma, blue sclerae, microcornea and marked myopia — the historical 'ocular-scoliotic' type.
A markedly increased urinary ratio of lysyl-pyridinoline to hydroxylysyl-pyridinoline cross-links is a specific, low-cost diagnostic pointer to the PLOD1 form (normal in the FKBP14 form).
The FKBP14 form is distinguished by congenital sensorineural or mixed hearing loss, a myopathy with muscle atrophy, and bladder diverticula.
Vascular fragility can cause rupture of medium-sized arteries; cardiovascular surveillance is warranted.
Skin is hyperextensible, soft, easily bruised and fragile with atrophic scarring, and osteopenia is common.
Distinguish from Marfan and Loeys-Dietz syndromes and from brittle cornea syndrome, which share overlapping features.
reference.pathophysiology: Kyphoscoliotic Ehlers-Danlos syndrome is an autosomal recessive disorder of collagen cross-linking and folding. In the commoner PLOD1 form, biallelic loss-of-function mutations abolish lysyl hydroxylase 1, the enzyme that hydroxylates specific lysine residues in the telopeptide and helical regions of collagen; these hydroxylysines are required to form stable pyridinoline intermolecular cross-links, so the resulting collagen is under-hydroxylated and inadequately cross-linked, weakening skin, ligaments, sclera, bone and the arterial wall. The biochemical signature is a shift in urinary cross-links, with lysyl-pyridinoline rising relative to hydroxylysyl-pyridinoline. In the FKBP14 form, loss of the endoplasmic reticulum peptidyl-prolyl cis-trans isomerase FKBP22, which acts as a folding chaperone for several collagens (notably types III, VI and X), leads to defective collagen maturation with a broadly similar connective-tissue fragility but additional myopathic and cochlear involvement. In both forms the connective tissue framework is mechanically incompetent, producing the characteristic neonatal hypotonia, progressive spinal deformity and joint instability.
additionalDifferentials: Other Ehlers-Danlos subtypes (classical, vascular and spondylodysplastic)
Brittle cornea syndrome (ZNF469 or PRDM5 related)
Congenital myopathies (particularly for the hypotonic FKBP14 form)
Congenital or syndromic scoliosis of other cause
additionalInvestigations: Urinary pyridinoline cross-link ratio (lysyl- to hydroxylysyl-pyridinoline) to identify the PLOD1 form
Molecular genetic testing of PLOD1 and FKBP14
Whole-spine imaging to characterise and monitor kyphoscoliosis
Echocardiography and arterial imaging for vascular fragility and aortic dimensions
Ophthalmological assessment of globe integrity, cornea and refraction
Audiological testing, especially in the FKBP14 form
redFlags: Ocular globe rupture or scleral perforation after minor trauma (PLOD1 form)
Rupture or dissection of medium-sized arteries
Rapidly progressive kyphoscoliosis with restrictive respiratory compromise
reference.prognosis: Outcome varies with subtype and severity; progressive kyphoscoliosis and consequent restrictive lung disease, together with vascular and (in the PLOD1 form) ocular rupture, drive morbidity and can shorten life, though many affected individuals reach adulthood with proactive surveillance.
pitfalls: Mislabelling the condition as Marfan or vascular Ehlers-Danlos owing to the marfanoid habitus and arterial risk
Failing to protect fragile eyes, allowing preventable globe rupture
Omitting the inexpensive, specific urinary cross-link ratio in a suspected PLOD1 case
Attributing neonatal hypotonia solely to a primary neuromuscular disorder
management: No specific curative therapy; core management is physiotherapy to strengthen muscle around hypermobile joints, orthotic bracing and low-impact conditioning to counter congenital hypotonia and protect against recurrent dislocation

Ascorbic acid (vitamin C) supplementation as a cofactor supporting residual collagen cross-linking in the PLOD1 form, alongside orthopaedic and spinal surgical correction of progressive kyphoscoliosis
Protective eye measures and prompt ophthalmology input for the scleral and globe fragility of the PLOD1 form, with correction of myopia and avoidance of ocular trauma
Cardiovascular surveillance with echocardiography and arterial imaging for aortic dilatation and medium-vessel fragility, with blood-pressure control to reduce arterial rupture risk
Respiratory monitoring for restrictive lung disease from progressive kyphoscoliosis, and audiology with hearing support in the FKBP14 form
Urgent surgical and vascular assessment for arterial or scleral/globe rupture, anticipating that tissue fragility complicates haemostasis and wound healing
Multidisciplinary coordination across clinical genetics, spinal surgery, cardiology, ophthalmology and physiotherapy
Genetic counselling with PLOD1/FKBP14 carrier testing and family screening given autosomal recessive inheritance
